title: Anyone else feel Montgomery Clift was the best of the original method actors?

commenti.body: As a self professed crybaby and a victim of bullying in his teens my grandfather said he related to james deans character so much in rebel without a cause- the title is a Dumb name when you think about. He had such good reason to rebel.
Have you seen East of Eden? Dean is phenomenal in it and it's my favorite performance of his.

There are some actors whose personality or story really distracts from the performance. It’s rare but… I’m just so disturbed by the story of the guy who tried to dig up Montgomery Clift. I get that he had epic sex parties but why are you digging up a dead body? I can’t watch him because I keep thinking of that guy who tried to dig him up. You really thought you could dig that deep into the ground? How were you going to open the casket? And then what? There’s no way of knowing. But I can’t watch him because I just think of that guy with a shovel.

Wtf!!?! Okay this is the first i'm hearing of this. When did this happen and where did you read about? Clift is buried in a private Quaker cemetery and I never had any desire to visit because I am not a family member and I try my best to respect other peoples privacy.
[removed]

I was told by the sex editor from Vogue in 2001. We grew up in the same town and were friends. The guy was obsessed with how handsome Clift was, and that he threw all of those sex parties. I can’t watch him because I get so distracted. Whatever happened to that guy who tried to dig up Montgomery Clift? I just keep wondering. What did the police charge him with? Trespassing? It’s a mystery that ruins him for me in film. I don’t get it. He died in 1966. Let’s say the guy dug down deep enough and got into the casket. He’s been dead for over 30 years at that point. I’m just so confused.

Well, there were people like Karl Malden and L.J Cobb who studied with Stella Adler or Lee Strasberg. But for some reason people think only of the heart throbs when it comes to the early "Method". Personally I think Paul Newman, who also studied under Adler is overlooked.

Cobb worked with Kazan and the group theatre, but he never studied with Robert Lewis, Stella Adler, or Lee Strasberg who were the big three method acting teachers from the 40's and 50's. Karl Malden had very brief uncredited one line roles in films until 1950 when he got supporting roles in The Gunfighter and Where the Sidewalk Ends. I think saying Clift's heartthrob status overrates his ranking is untrue. After his car accident when he was no longer had that he still put in great performances. As for Paul Newman he didn't become famous until after Clift, Brando, and Dean debuted so that's why he isn't usually grouped with them even though I feel he was good and does qualify as a method actor.

I don't doubt what your saying, but there is no mention of this anywhere online. This is the first i'm hearing of this and I'm just as creeped out by it as you are. I'm a huge Clift fan, but I would never even visit his grave let alone think of doing what that guy did. I hope he's in jail. What a creep.

From what I gather, there's an evolution from group theater to figures like Lewis, Adler, and Strasberg. The concept of the "Method" originally stemmed from Stanislawsky in Russia, although my memory on the details isn't very fresh. By the way, there's an amusing video on YouTube featuring James Dean and Paul Newman doing screen tests for East of Eden.

I understand what your saying and to be clear I'm not arguing that you are wrong and appreciate your input. I think when we get into a discussion of "method acting" it is very subjective and debatable. For example I know John Garfield (like Cobb) also studied with the Group theatre and some consider him the first method actor although I don't necessarily agree with that I can't say anyone is wrong for believing that. I just felt Clift, Brando and Dean represented something unique and different that hadn't really been seen before in cinema and there's a reason those three are usually grouped together. Also I have seen that East of Eden screen test with Dean and Newman and found it hilarious how they were playfully teasing each other. I think Newman would have been good in it had he been cast as Cal's brother.

Mine, too. He’s so good in that.

Also loved his performance in “Giant.”

All great actors but agree Clift may have been the best.

Also loved his performance in “The Misfits,” particularly that phone both scene.


He also helped coax a very good performance from John Wayne in “Red River.” Wayne knew if he didn’t raise his game the kid would blow him off the screen. 😂
Loved Newman in “The Hustler” and “Hud” especially.

The Criterion Channel had an awesome filmed conversation about Method Acting up a little while ago, and you could definitely feel that Vincent D'Onofrio, one of the participants, thought so. He criticized Brando and Dean for not really being pure method at all and for dominating their stories. Streetcar is meant to be all about Blanche, but Brando turned every scene into the Stanley Kowalski show. Clift in A Place in the Sun was offered as a counterexample.
[removed]

Strasberg was one of the founders of the Group Theatre and was the one training the actors. So yeah, Lee J Cobb studied with him. 

Malden was also in the Group Theatre and was part of the original group of people when the Actors Studio was created by Lewis and Kazan. 

Clift, from what I’ve read, didn’t spend much time at all with any of these teachers.

If you liked that movie as much as me I highly recommend the book which is one of my all time favorites. There’s another half of the story that’s not in the film, and the whole book is just such a vibe

Strasberg was one of the founders of the Group Theatre and was the one training the actors there. So Lee J Cobb studied with him.

Malden was also a member of the Group Theatre and was part of the initial class at the Actors Studio.

Clift was also a part of the initial class but from what I’ve heard didn’t spend much time there. I don’t think he actually trained much at all with Robert Lewis.

Also, Uta Hagen and Sanford Meisner were probably bigger method teachers than Robert Lewis.
[removed]

montgomery clift was a powerhouse. his performances had a depth and vulnerability that set him apart. it's tragic how his personal struggles cut his career short. all three of them were incredibly talented, but clift's impact shouldn't be overlooked.
